blocks.text: A sprinter crosses the finish line of a 400 m race. During the race the ATP demand in her leg muscle rose many-fold within seconds, yet the mitochondria in those cells matched the demand without any conscious signal. The hub that connects burning of food-derived acetyl-CoA to the supply of reduced coenzymes for ATP production is the citric acid cycle. How does the cycle sense energy status, and what else does the cell take from it?

blocks.markdown: The **citric acid cycle** (also called the tricarboxylic acid or Krebs cycle) is a closed loop of eight enzyme-catalysed reactions in the **mitochondrial matrix** (succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane). It oxidises the acetyl group of **acetyl-CoA**, which comes from carbohydrate, fat and amino acid breakdown, completely to CO2. The energy is captured as reduced coenzymes (NADH and FADH2), which pass electrons to the respiratory chain, and as one high-energy phosphate. The cycle needs oxygen only indirectly, because NAD+ and FAD must be regenerated by the electron transport chain, so it stops without oxygen.

blocks.title: Citric acid cycle
blocks.text: The citric acid cycle is the mitochondrial pathway in which the two-carbon acetyl group of acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) to make citrate (6C); two carbons are then removed as CO2 and oxaloacetate is regenerated, producing NADH, FADH2 and GTP (or ATP).

rows: Isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate (5C): CO2 released, NADH formed
Alpha-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA (4C): CO2 released, NADH formed
Succinyl-CoA to succinate: GTP (or ATP) formed by substrate-level phosphorylation
Succinate to fumarate: FADH2 formed (also Complex II of the respiratory chain)
Malate to oxaloacetate: NADH formed, cycle regenerated
blocks.caption: The eight reactions of the citric acid cycle.
Net equation for one turn of the cycle (the acetyl group of one acetyl-CoA).

blocks.markdown: **Reading the net equation.** One turn consumes one acetyl-CoA and yields **3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO2**. The two CO2 come from the isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps. Oxaloacetate is not consumed: it is regenerated, so in principle a small amount of oxaloacetate can oxidise unlimited acetyl-CoA. When the reduced coenzymes are oxidised by the respiratory chain, each NADH gives about 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 about 1.5 ATP (commonly used values; some textbooks use 3 and 2).

blocks.title: ATP equivalents from one turn of the cycle
blocks.prompt: Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH2 and 1 ATP per GTP, calculate the ATP equivalents produced per acetyl-CoA oxidised in the cycle.

steps.text: Count outputs per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP.
Convert each: 3 x 2.5 = 7.5 ATP from NADH; 1 x 1.5 = 1.5 ATP from FADH2; 1 ATP from GTP.

blocks.answer: About 10 ATP per acetyl-CoA, nearly all (9 of the 10) generated indirectly via the respiratory chain.

blocks.markdown:
**Regulation by energy status.** The cycle is controlled at three irreversible, exergonic steps, and its flux matches the cell's energy needs mainly through product inhibition and activation by low-energy signals:

- **Citrate synthase** is inhibited by its products citrate and by high ATP and NADH, and limited by availability of oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA.
- **Isocitrate dehydrogenase** is the main control point: it is activated by ADP and by Ca2+, and inhibited by ATP and NADH.
- **Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase** is inhibited by its products NADH and succinyl-CoA and by high energy charge, and activated by Ca2+.

When ATP and NADH are high (resting, well-fed cell), flux slows. In contracting muscle, ADP and Ca2+ rise and speed the cycle at the same moment as demand rises. Because NADH accumulates when the respiratory chain is limited (for example by lack of oxygen), the cycle also slows without oxygen.

blocks.caption: Regulation of the citric acid cycle by energy status.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of a rise in NADH
blocks.prompt: A hepatocyte is rich in ATP and its NADH/NAD+ ratio is high. Predict what happens to the flux of the cycle and explain which enzymes mediate the change.

steps.text: High NADH inhibits isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase directly (product inhibition).
High ATP also inhibits isocitrate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase, reducing both entry of acetyl-CoA and the oxidative steps.
Low ADP removes the activating signal on isocitrate dehydrogenase. All the regulatory signals point in the same direction.

blocks.answer: Cycle flux decreases, mediated mainly by isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; acetyl-CoA is diverted to storage (for example fatty acid synthesis).

blocks.markdown: **Biosynthetic roles and anaplerosis.** The cycle is not only a combustion pathway. Its intermediates are precursors for many molecules: **citrate** leaves the mitochondrion (cytosolic ATP-citrate lyase then regenerates acetyl-CoA) for **fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis**; **alpha-ketoglutarate** gives **glutamate** (and glutamine); **oxaloacetate** gives **aspartate** and, via gluconeogenesis, glucose; **succinyl-CoA** is a precursor of **haem** (with glycine). Withdrawal of intermediates would drain the cycle, so they must be replaced by **anaplerotic** reactions. The most important is **pyruvate carboxylase**, a biotin-requiring enzyme that converts pyruvate and CO2 to oxaloacetate, using ATP, and is activated by acetyl-CoA.

items: One turn: 1 acetyl-CoA in; 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP and 2 CO2 out.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are the CO2-releasing steps and the key regulated points.
ATP and NADH slow the cycle; ADP and Ca2+ speed it.
Intermediates leave for biosynthesis (citrate: fatty acids; alpha-ketoglutarate: glutamate; oxaloacetate: aspartate and glucose; succinyl-CoA: haem) and are replaced by anaplerosis.

blocks.title: Where the cycle's carbons come from
blocks.text: The two CO2 released in a given turn do not come from the acetyl group that entered in that same turn; they come from carbons of the oxaloacetate-derived part of the molecule. The acetyl carbons are lost in later turns. Do not state that the acetyl carbons are released as CO2 in the first turn.

points: One turn of the cycle oxidises one acetyl-CoA to 2 CO2, giving 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP (about 10 ATP equivalents).
Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are regulated by ATP, NADH, ADP and Ca2+, so flux follows energy demand.
Intermediates supply fatty acid, amino acid, glucose and haem synthesis; anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase replenish oxaloacetate.

questions.stem: Which combination of products is formed by one complete turn of the citric acid cycle from one acetyl-CoA?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the three NADH come from isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.b: This gives the wrong stoichiometry; only one FADH2 and one GTP form per turn.
distractorRationale.c: FADH2 is formed only by succinate dehydrogenase, so there is one, not three.
distractorRationale.d: There are two decarboxylation steps, so two CO2, and only one substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.explanation: NADH is formed at isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase, FADH2 at succinate dehydrogenase, GTP at succinyl-CoA synthetase, and CO2 at the first two dehydrogenases. This matches the net equation of the cycle.

questions.stem: Which reaction of the citric acid cycle produces a high-energy phosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the thioester to GDP (or ADP) phosphorylation.
distractorRationale.b: This step produces NADH and CO2, with no phosphate bond formed.
distractorRationale.c: This is a hydration with no energy-conserving product.
distractorRationale.d: This produces NADH, which yields ATP only later in the respiratory chain.

questions.explanation: The energy of the thioester bond of succinyl-CoA is used directly to phosphorylate GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP) by succinyl-CoA synthetase. This is substrate-level phosphorylation. The other steps conserve energy as NADH or FADH2 or not at all.

questions.stem: A muscle cell at rest has high ATP and NADH and low ADP. Which prediction about citric acid cycle activity is correct?

options.text: Flux decreases because ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase and NADH inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Flux increases because NADH activates isocitrate dehydrogenase
Flux is unchanged because the cycle is not regulated
Flux increases because low ADP activates citrate synthase

questions.correctOptionText: Flux decreases because ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase and NADH inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: high energy status slows the dehydrogenases.
distractorRationale.b: NADH inhibits, not activates, isocitrate dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.c: The cycle is regulated at several enzymes.
distractorRationale.d: Low ADP removes the activating signal on isocitrate dehydrogenase; citrate synthase is not activated by low ADP.

questions.explanation: ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase, and NADH and succinyl-CoA inhibit alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Low ADP removes activation. The result is slowed flux in a well-supplied, resting cell.

questions.stem: During sprinting, cytosolic Ca2+ released for muscle contraction also enters mitochondria. What effect does the rise in mitochondrial Ca2+ have on the cycle?

options.text: It activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, matching ATP production to the work being done
It inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, protecting the cell from acidosis
It converts the cycle into an anaplerotic pathway
It inhibits citrate synthase so that citrate is exported for fatty acid synthesis

questions.correctOptionText: It activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, matching ATP production to the work being done

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Ca2+ is a feed-forward activator signalling increased demand.
distractorRationale.b: Ca2+ does not inhibit succinate dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.c: Anaplerosis refers to replenishing intermediates, not to Ca2+ action.
distractorRationale.d: Ca2+ is not an inhibitor of citrate synthase, and fatty acid synthesis is not favoured during exercise.

questions.explanation: Ca2+ activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, together with ADP. This links the contraction signal to a faster cycle, increasing NADH supply for the respiratory chain.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a cycle intermediate with a biosynthetic product it supplies is correct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: succinyl-CoA condenses with glycine to begin haem synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Fatty acid synthesis uses citrate exported to the cytosol, not fumarate.
distractorRationale.c: Glutamate comes from alpha-ketoglutarate; malate leads to oxaloacetate.
distractorRationale.d: Aspartate comes from oxaloacetate, not isocitrate.

questions.explanation: Succinyl-CoA with glycine starts haem synthesis. Citrate supplies cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty acids and cholesterol, alpha-ketoglutarate gives glutamate, and oxaloacetate gives aspartate.

questions.stem: True or false: oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of each turn of the citric acid cycle and is therefore not consumed by the acetyl-CoA oxidation itself.
questions.explanation: Malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate at the last step, so oxaloacetate acts catalytically. Only acetyl-CoA is consumed. The cycle can lose oxaloacetate only when intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis.

questions.stem: A biochemist isolates mitochondrial inner membranes and finds that one enzyme of the citric acid cycle is embedded in the membrane and also serves as a complex of the respiratory chain. Which enzyme is it?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is Complex II and produces FADH2 from succinate.
distractorRationale.b: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a matrix enzyme that produces NADH.
distractorRationale.c: Fumarase is a soluble matrix enzyme that hydrates fumarate.
distractorRationale.d: Citrate synthase is a soluble matrix enzyme that forms citrate.

questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only citric acid cycle enzyme bound to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it acts as Complex II of the respiratory chain. It passes electrons from succinate (via FAD) to ubiquinone, so one turn of the cycle yields one FADH2 equivalent.

questions.stem: A mitochondrion oxidises 6 molecules of acetyl-CoA through the citric acid cycle. Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH2 and 1 ATP per GTP, calculate the total ATP equivalents generated from the cycle and its reduced coenzymes.
questions.explanation: Each turn gives 3 NADH (7.5 ATP), 1 FADH2 (1.5 ATP) and 1 GTP (1 ATP), totalling 10 ATP equivalents. Six acetyl-CoA therefore give 6 x 10 = 60 ATP. These values assume the P/O ratios stated; some textbooks use 3 and 2 per NADH and FADH2.

questions.stem: Identify the main points at which the citric acid cycle is regulated and explain how each responds to the energy status of the cell.
markingGuide: Citrate synthase: inhibited by citrate, high ATP and NADH, limited by substrate availability
Isocitrate dehydrogenase: activated by ADP and Ca2+, inhibited by ATP and NADH; the main control point
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase: inhibited by NADH and succinyl-CoA, activated by Ca2+
High energy status (high ATP and NADH) slows the cycle; low energy status (high ADP) or Ca2+ signalling for work speeds it
Indirect control: NAD+ and FAD must be regenerated by the respiratory chain, so lack of oxygen raises NADH and slows the cycle
questions.explanation: The cycle is controlled by the products of the cell's energy metabolism: ATP and NADH inhibit the dehydrogenases, while ADP and Ca2+ activate them. This keeps NADH production matched to the rate at which the respiratory chain can use it.

questions.stem: A liver cell is withdrawing oxaloacetate from the cycle for gluconeogenesis during a fast. Explain why the cycle would stall without a mechanism to replace it, how the cell replaces it, and name two other biosynthetic products drawn from cycle intermediates.
markingGuide: Oxaloacetate is needed to accept acetyl-CoA in citrate synthase; withdrawal lowers its concentration and slows the cycle
Replenishment (anaplerosis) by pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO2 + ATP gives oxaloacetate, requires biotin
Pyruvate carboxylase is activated by acetyl-CoA, which signals that oxaloacetate is needed
Two examples from: citrate to fatty acids or cholesterol; alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate; oxaloacetate to aspartate; succinyl-CoA to haem
questions.explanation: Intermediates drawn off for synthesis must be replaced or the cycle runs out of oxaloacetate, the acceptor of acetyl-CoA. Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate and is stimulated by acetyl-CoA, so the cycle is replenished exactly when acetyl-CoA is abundant.
